chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Nu'aym ibn Ibrahim, from Misma' ibn Abdul Malik, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The mother of the child (umm al-walad), her crimes regarding the rights of people are upon her master, and whatever of the Rights of Allah (Exalted and Majestic) is in the legal penalties (hudud), then that is upon her body. He said: And retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is taken from her for the slaves, and there is no retaliation between the free and the slave.

key_terms.أُمُّ الْوَلَدِ: A female slave who bears a child to her master, gaining specific legal status
key_terms.الْحُدُودِ: Legal penalties prescribed in Islamic law for specific crimes
key_terms.حُقُوقِ اللَّهِ: Rights of God, typically involving fixed legal penalties (hudud)
key_terms.حُقُوقِ النَّاسِ: Rights of people, typically involving financial compensation or property
key_terms.يُقَاصُّ: Retaliation (qiṣāṣ), specifically in the context of retribution for murder or injury

ai.seo_question: Who bears the financial liability for the crimes of a slave mother (umm al-walad) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the distinct legal liabilities of an 'umm al-walad' by distinguishing between financial compensation for the master (ḥuqū al-nās) and corporal punishment for divine limits (ḥudūd). It further establishes the principle of asymmetrical retaliation (qiṣāṣ) between free persons and slaves, a key topic in Shia jurisprudence regarding social hierarchy and justice. The ruling reflects the practical application of Quranic verses on retribution within the specific context of the slave-master relationship.
